assessment_summary: The author's explanation of the converse proof contains a mathematical error regarding the number of bipartite graphs. In lines 74 and 78, the author claims that combining the bipartite graphs from subsets X and Y yields 2^{k-1} bipartite graphs, while seemingly expecting 2^k. In reality, combining the (k-1) bipartite graphs from X with the (k-1) bipartite graphs from Y pairwise yields exactly k-1 bipartite graphs. The author appears to have confused the number of bipartite graphs (k-1) with the size bound of the vertex subsets (2^{k-1}).
counterexample: Let k=3, so n=8 (which satisfies n <= 2^3). We partition the vertex set of K_8 into subsets X and Y, each of size 4. The complete subgraph on X (K_4) is covered by k-1 = 2 bipartite graphs, say X_1 and X_2. The complete subgraph on Y (K_4) is covered by k-1 = 2 bipartite graphs, say Y_1 and Y_2. By combining the i-th bipartite graph on X with the i-th bipartite graph on Y (i.e., taking the unions X_1 U Y_1 and X_2 U Y_2), we obtain exactly k-1 = 2 bipartite graphs. However, the claim in line 78 asserts we get "2^{k-1} bipartite graphs". For k=3, this evaluates to 2^{3-1} = 4, which falsely contradicts the actual count of 2 bipartite graphs.
